papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that reasoning models dynamically refine internal representations of actions and predicates during extended reasoning, and these refined representations causally improve problem-solving performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that reasoning models' superior performance on abstract reasoning tasks may stem from their ability to dynamically construct context-specific representational spaces during extended reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
QwQ-32B progressively adapts internal representations of actions and predicates during reasoning, converging toward consistent encodings regardless of initial action names.
These representational adaptations causally improve problem-solving performance: injecting refined representations from successful traces boosts accuracy.
Adapted representations achieve symbolic abstraction, enabling cross-naming transfer and minimal performance loss when replaced with symbolic representations.
papers.limitation:
Focus on a single reasoning model (QwQ-32B) and a single domain (BlocksWorld).
Steering and patching intervention methods are deliberately simple and coarse.
Computational limits prevented extensive hyperparameter sweeps or decoding strategy comparisons.
future_direction: Verifying generalization to other structured planning setups and less constrained domains.
Using more targeted or fine-grained causal tools.
Explaining late-layer representational dynamics.
papers.abstract: Reasoning language models, which generate long chains of thought, dramatically outperform non-reasoning language models on abstract problems. However, the internal model mechanisms that allow this superior performance remain poorly understood. We present a mechanistic analysis of how QwQ-32B - a model specifically trained to produce extensive reasoning traces - process abstract structural information. On Mystery Blocksworld - a semantically obfuscated planning domain - we find that QwQ-32B gradually improves its internal representation of actions and concepts during reasoning. The model develops abstract encodings that focus on structure rather than specific action names. Through steering experiments, we establish causal evidence that these adaptations improve problem solving: injecting refined representations from successful traces boosts accuracy, while symbolic representations can replace many obfuscated encodings with minimal performance loss. We find that one of the factors driving reasoning model performance is in-context refinement of token representations, which we dub Fluid Reasoning Representations.

papers.title: exBERT: A Visual Analysis Tool to Explore Learned Representations in Transformers Models
papers.research_question: How to interactively explore and understand what attention heads in transformer models have learned, specifically in BERT, by combining attention visualization with nearest neighbor search on annotated corpora.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces EXBERT, an interactive visualization tool that uses linguistic annotations, interactive masking, and nearest neighbor search to explore and explain learned representations and attention mechanisms in transformer models.
papers.conclusion: EXBERT is an interactive visualization tool that uses linguistic annotations, interactive masking, and nearest neighbor search to reveal intelligible structure in learned representations of transformer models, demonstrated with BERT on the Wizard of Oz corpus.
papers.key_findings:
At early layers (e.g., layer 1), masked token embeddings show similarity to common tokens like punctuation and determinants, with no meaningful linguistic information encoded.
As layers progress, more part-of-speech information is added; by layer 6, BERT becomes confident that a masked token is a verb, refining this estimation in later layers.
Complex dependencies such as direct object (DOBJ) are detected in early-middle layers but rely on a combination of multiple attention heads, not individual heads.
Positional heads attend to succeeding or preceding tokens and encode linguistic information about the attended-to word, such as part-of-speech and dependency relations.
EXBERT enables interactive exploration of how attention heads contribute to encoding linguistic features in token embeddings through nearest neighbor search on annotated corpora.
papers.abstract: Large language models can produce powerful contextual representations that lead to improvements across many NLP tasks. Since these models are typically guided by a sequence of learned self attention mechanisms and may comprise undesired inductive biases, it is paramount to be able to explore what the attention has learned. While static analyses of these models lead to targeted insights, interactive tools are more dynamic and can help humans better gain an intuition for the model-internal reasoning process. We present exBERT, an interactive tool named after the popular BERT language model, that provides insights into the meaning of the contextual representations by matching a human-specified input to similar contexts in a large annotated dataset. By aggregating the annotations of the matching similar contexts, exBERT helps intuitively explain what each attention-head has learned.

papers.title: Can Aha Moments Be Fake? Identifying True and Decorative Thinking Steps in Chain-of-Thought
papers.research_question: To what extent do LLMs truly think through each verbalized step in their chain-of-thought (CoT)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the True Thinking Score (TTS) to quantify the causal contribution of each step in chain-of-thought reasoning, revealing that LLMs often interleave true-thinking steps with decorative ones, and identifies a steerable 'TrueThinking' direction in latent space that controls whether a step is internally followed.
papers.conclusion: LLMs often verbalize reasoning steps without performing them internally, challenging the efficiency of LLM reasoning and the trustworthiness of chain-of-thought as a safety-monitoring signal.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs often interleave true-thinking steps (which causally affect the final prediction) and decorative-thinking steps (which have minimal causal influence).
Only a small subset of reasoning steps causally drive the model's prediction; e.g., on AIME, only an average of 2.3% of steps have TTS ≥ 0.7 for Qwen-2.5.
Self-verification steps (aha moments) in CoT can be decorative, meaning the model does not truly check its solution internally.
A linear 'TrueThinking' direction in latent space can mediate whether LLMs internally reason over a verbalized step; steering along this direction forces engagement, while reversing it suppresses step use.
The latent signal controlling step engagement is universal across datasets and model sizes, with intermediate layers (e.g., 15-22 in Qwen) concentrating reasoning-related representations.
future_direction: Future study to explain the mechanisms of CoT reasoning and develop training objectives that reward reliance on true-thinking steps.
In-depth study of the geometry of hidden states and TrueThinking directions in the latent space.
papers.abstract: Large language models can generate long chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning, but it remains unclear whether the verbalized steps reflect the models' internal thinking. In this work, we propose a True Thinking Score (TTS) to quantify the causal contribution of each step in CoT to the model's final prediction. Our experiments show that LLMs often interleave between true-thinking steps (which are genuinely used to compute the final output) and decorative-thinking steps (which give the appearance of reasoning but have minimal causal influence). We reveal that only a small subset of the total reasoning steps causally drive the model's prediction: e.g., on AIME, only an average of 2.3% of reasoning steps in CoT have a TTS >= 0.7 (range: 0-1) for Qwen-2.5. Furthermore, we find that LLMs can be steered to internally follow or disregard specific steps in their verbalized CoT using the identified TrueThinking direction. We highlight that self-verification steps in CoT (i.e., aha moments) can be decorative, while steering along the TrueThinking direction can force internal reasoning over these steps. Overall, our work reveals that LLMs often verbalize reasoning steps without performing them internally, challenging the efficiency of LLM reasoning and the trustworthiness of CoT.

papers.title: Reasoning Beyond Words ? Exploring framework for hidden state reasoning
papers.research_question: Can reasoning in a continuous latent space, as opposed to the language space, lead to more efficient and effective reasoning in LLMs, particularly for tasks requiring planning and search?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Coconut, a method for reasoning in a continuous latent space by feeding the last hidden state back as the next input embedding, which enables emergent tree search behavior and improves reasoning efficiency and accuracy on certain tasks.
papers.conclusion: Reasoning in latent space leads to advanced emergent behaviors like BFS, and Coconut enhances LLM performance across reasoning tasks, with potential for future scaling and research.
papers.key_findings:
Coconut outperforms CoT on logical reasoning tasks that require planning and search (ProsQA).
Continuous thoughts can encode multiple alternative next steps, enabling a breadth-first search (BFS) pattern.
Coconut provides a better trade-off between accuracy and efficiency (fewer tokens) compared to CoT.
The multi-stage training curriculum is crucial for learning latent reasoning; without it, performance drops.
Increasing the number of continuous thoughts per reasoning step (c) can improve performance up to a point.
papers.limitation:
Training requires a multi-stage curriculum; without it, performance drops significantly.
Larger models (Llama) show less pronounced gains, possibly due to extensive language-focused pre-training.
Training efficiency is challenging due to sequential forward passes, limiting parallelism.
future_direction: Refine and scale latent reasoning to pretraining for better generalization.
Combine iCoT and Coconut for improved training.
Develop better strategies for learning reasoning in latent space without supervision from language reasoning chains.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are typically constrained to reason in the language space, where they express the reasoning process through a chain-of-thought (CoT) to solve complex problems. However, the language space may not always be optimal for reasoning. Most word tokens primarily ensure textual coherence and are not essential for reasoning, while some critical tokens require complex planning and pose challenges to LLMs. To explore the potential of reasoning beyond language, we introduce a new paradigm called Coconut (Chain of Continuous Thought). Coconut utilizes the last hidden state of the LLM as a representation of the reasoning state, termed "continuous thought." Instead of decoding this state into words, we feed it back to the model as the next input embedding directly in the continuous space. This latent reasoning paradigm enables an advanced reasoning pattern, where continuous thoughts can encode multiple alternative next steps, allowing the model to perform a breadth-first search (BFS) rather than committing prematurely to a single deterministic path as in CoT. Coconut outperforms CoT on logical reasoning tasks that require substantial search during planning and achieves a better trade-off between accuracy and efficiency.

papers.title: Multiple Token Divergence: Measuring and Steering In-Context Computation Density
papers.research_question: How can we measure the in-context computational effort of language models, and can we use this measure to steer generation?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Multiple Token Divergence (MTD), a simple measure of computational effort based on KL divergence between full model and shallow auxiliary head predictions, and introduces Divergence Steering, a decoding method to steer generation towards or away from computationally dense tokens.
papers.conclusion: MTD provides a practical, non-invasive measure of computational effort, and Divergence Steering allows controlling the computational character of generated text, complementing temperature-based decoding.
papers.key_findings:
MTD effectively distinguishes complex tasks from simple ones.
MTD correlates positively with problem difficulty in mathematical reasoning.
Lower MTD is associated with more accurate reasoning.
Divergence Steering can improve performance on creative tasks.
MTD is more robust and easier to compute than prior methods like PHi loss.
papers.limitation:
MTD depends on the relative capacities of the main model and MTP module; if the MTP module is too powerful, MTD approaches zero, and if too weak, MTD offers little beyond NLL.
MTD may conflate genuine computational effort with simple patterns that exceed the capacity of the lightweight shortcut.
The relationship between computational effort and correctness is complex and model-dependent.
future_direction: Dynamic compute allocation based on MTD monitoring.
Using MTD as a signal for solution convergence.
Employing MTD as an intrinsic reward in agent-based settings.
Using MTD and Divergence Steering to filter or generate 'interesting' data for open-ended learning.
papers.abstract: Measuring the in-context computational effort of language models is a key challenge, as metrics like next-token loss fail to capture reasoning complexity. Prior methods based on latent state compressibility can be invasive and unstable. We propose Multiple Token Divergence (MTD), a simple measure of computational effort defined as the KL divergence between a model's full output distribution and that of a shallow, auxiliary prediction head. MTD can be computed directly from pre-trained models with multiple prediction heads, requiring no additional training. Building on this, we introduce Divergence Steering, a novel decoding method to control the computational character of generated text. We empirically show that MTD is more effective than prior methods at distinguishing complex tasks from simple ones. On mathematical reasoning benchmarks, MTD correlates positively with problem difficulty. Lower MTD is associated with more accurate reasoning. MTD provides a practical, lightweight tool for analyzing and steering the computational dynamics of language models.

papers.title: Efficient Reasoning with Hidden Thinking
papers.research_question: How can we make Chain-of-Thought reasoning more efficient by encoding intermediate reasoning steps into compact hidden representations?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Heima, an efficient reasoning framework that encodes Chain-of-Thought reasoning steps into compact hidden representations (thinking tokens) within a multimodal large language model, significantly reducing token generation while maintaining or improving task accuracy.
papers.conclusion: Heima provides an efficient and interpretable framework for multimodal reasoning by performing hidden thinking in the latent space, achieving high reasoning efficiency with significantly fewer tokens while maintaining strong task performance.
papers.key_findings:
Heima reduces the number of generated tokens to as little as 6% of the original while maintaining comparable or superior accuracy on zero-shot reasoning benchmarks.
Progressive encoding (gradually converting CoT stages to thinking tokens) and a final recovering stage are crucial for maintaining model performance.
The Heima Decoder can effectively reconstruct the original reasoning processes from the hidden thinking tokens, validating the interpretability and robustness of the encoded representations.
Using a single thinking token per CoT stage yields the best performance, and adaptive encoding (varying the number of tokens based on original CoT length) does not show consistent benefits.
The framework is compatible with existing efficient inference techniques like KV cache optimization and flash attention.
future_direction: Extend the method to larger models for Heima Encoder
Explore the use of smaller LLMs as Heima Decoder to support diverse scale designs
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning has become a powerful framework for improving complex problem-solving capabilities in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). However, the verbose nature of textual reasoning introduces significant inefficiencies. In this work, we propose $\textbf{Heima}$ (as hidden llama), an efficient reasoning framework that leverages reasoning CoTs at hidden latent space. We design the Heima Encoder to condense each intermediate CoT into a compact, higher-level hidden representation using a single thinking token, effectively minimizing verbosity and reducing the overall number of tokens required during the reasoning process. Meanwhile, we design corresponding Heima Decoder with traditional Large Language Models (LLMs) to adaptively interpret the hidden representations into variable-length textual sequence, reconstructing reasoning processes that closely resemble the original CoTs. Experimental results across diverse reasoning MLLM benchmarks demonstrate that Heima model achieves higher generation efficiency while maintaining or even better zero-shot task accuracy. Moreover, the effective reconstruction of multimodal reasoning processes with Heima Decoder validates both the robustness and interpretability of our approach.

papers.title: ThinkEdit: Interpretable Weight Editing to Mitigate Overly Short Thinking in Reasoning Models
papers.abstract: Recent studies have shown that Large Language Models (LLMs) augmented with chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning demonstrate impressive problem-solving abilities. However, in this work, we identify a recurring issue where these models occasionally generate overly short reasoning, leading to degraded performance on even simple mathematical problems. Specifically, we investigate how reasoning length is embedded in the hidden representations of reasoning models and its impact on accuracy. Our analysis reveals that reasoning length is governed by a linear direction in the representation space, allowing us to induce overly short reasoning by steering the model along this direction. Building on this insight, we introduce ThinkEdit, a simple yet effective weight-editing approach to mitigate the issue of overly short reasoning. We first identify a small subset of attention heads (approximately 4%) that predominantly drive short reasoning behavior. We then edit the output projection weights of these heads to remove the short reasoning direction. With changes to only 0.2% of the model's parameters, ThinkEdit effectively reduces overly short reasoning and yields notable accuracy gains for short reasoning outputs (+6.39%), along with an overall improvement across multiple math benchmarks (+3.34%). Our findings provide new mechanistic insights into how reasoning length is controlled within LLMs and highlight the potential of fine-grained model interventions to improve reasoning quality. Our code is available at: https://github.com/Trustworthy-ML-Lab/ThinkEdit

papers.title: Enhancing Transformer Architecture: Techniques for Efficient Inference
papers.research_question: How can transformer architectures be optimized for efficient inference while preserving performance through techniques like pruning, quantization, and novel attention mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Dynamic Sparse Attention (DSA) and demonstrates that combining pruning, quantization, and DSA can significantly reduce inference time and memory usage while maintaining high performance, enabling deployment in resource-constrained environments.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a comprehensive analysis of efficiency techniques for transformers, showing that combining pruning, quantization, and DSA reduces inference time by up to 74% and memory usage by 80% while preserving over 91% performance, with practical applications for edge deployment.
papers.key_findings:
Combining pruning, quantization, and DSA reduces inference time by up to 74% while maintaining over 95% of original performance.
Dynamic Sparse Attention outperforms other sparse attention methods for long sequences.
On edge devices like Raspberry Pi 4, optimized models achieve a 3.7x speedup with only 7.4% reduction in accuracy.
DSA shows advantages in long document processing, outperforming specialized models like Longformer and BigBird.
Ablation studies confirm each component contributes meaningfully to the efficiency-performance trade-off.
papers.limitation:
Training Overhead: The importance scorer in Dynamic Sparse Attention requires additional training time compared to fixed patterns.
Hardware Adaptivity: Some optimizations like unstructured pruning show theoretical benefits but limited practical gains due to current hardware limitations.
Task Sensitivity: The optimal efficiency configuration varies significantly across tasks, suggesting a need for task-specific optimization.
future_direction: Hardware-Aware Optimization
Adaptive Compression
Learned Sparsity Patterns
papers.abstract: This paper explores recent advancements in optimizing transformer architectures for efficient inference. We investigate various techniques including pruning, quantization, knowledge distillation, and architectural modifications. Our experimental results demonstrate that combining these approaches can reduce inference time by up to 74% while maintaining over 95% of the original performance. We also introduce a novel attention mechanism that dynamically allocates computational resources based on input complexity. Our implementation shows promise for edge device deployment where computational resources are constrained.

papers.title: Seq-VCR: Preventing Collapse in Intermediate Transformer Representations for Enhanced Reasoning
papers.research_question: How does representation collapse in intermediate transformer layers limit reasoning capabilities, and can a regularization technique prevent this collapse to improve performance on complex reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Seq-VCR, a regularization technique that prevents representation collapse in intermediate transformer layers, and shows that combining it with pause tokens improves reasoning performance without explicit chain-of-thought supervision.
papers.conclusion: Intermediate layer representation collapse detrimentally affects the computation of intermediate information essential for solving arithmetic reasoning tasks, and Seq-VCR enhances the model's representation capacity to improve its ability to solve these tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Seq-VCR prevents representation collapse and increases entropy in intermediate transformer layers.
Seq-VCR combined with pause tokens achieves 99.5% exact match accuracy on 5x5 digit multiplication, outperforming same-size models (0%) and GPT-4 with CoT (44%).
Seq-VCR improves performance on arithmetic expression and longest increasing subsequence (LIS) datasets.
Representation collapse is identified as a key factor limiting transformer reasoning capabilities.
Seq-VCR enables models to solve complex reasoning tasks without explicit chain-of-thought supervision.
papers.limitation: Pause tokens share the same embedding, which may limit their effectiveness.
future_direction: Explore the effect of having different embeddings per pause token.
Enhance pre-training with improved representation learning to increase model capabilities.
papers.abstract: Decoder-only Transformers often struggle with complex reasoning tasks, particularly arithmetic reasoning requiring multiple sequential operations. In this work, we identify representation collapse in the model's intermediate layers as a key factor limiting their reasoning capabilities. To address this, we propose Sequential Variance-Covariance Regularization (Seq-VCR), which enhances the entropy of intermediate representations and prevents collapse. Combined with dummy pause tokens as substitutes for chain-of-thought (CoT) tokens, our method significantly improves performance in arithmetic reasoning problems. In the challenging $5 \times 5$ integer multiplication task, our approach achieves $99.5\%$ exact match accuracy, outperforming models of the same size (which yield $0\%$ accuracy) and GPT-4 with five-shot CoT prompting ($44\%$). We also demonstrate superior results on arithmetic expression and longest increasing subsequence (LIS) datasets. Our findings highlight the importance of preventing intermediate layer representation collapse to enhance the reasoning capabilities of Transformers and show that Seq-VCR offers an effective solution without requiring explicit CoT supervision.

papers.title: Measuring the Mixing of Contextual Information in the Transformer
papers.research_question: How is contextual information mixed across the Transformer architecture, and how can this mixing be measured to provide faithful explanations for model predictions?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes ALTI, an interpretability method that measures token-to-token interactions within each Transformer layer and aggregates them to provide input attribution scores, demonstrating more faithful explanations and increased robustness than gradient-based methods.
papers.conclusion: ALTI is a powerful interpretability method that quantifies the mixing of information in the Transformer, providing faithful input attributions and opening new possibilities for studying contextual information aggregation.
papers.key_findings:
ALTI outperforms gradient-based and other attribution methods in faithfulness metrics (comprehensiveness and sufficiency) across multiple models and datasets.
ALTI provides more robust interpretations across models with identical architecture but different random initializations, as measured by Jaccard similarity and Spearman correlation.
Using ℓ1 norm for measuring token contributions in ALTI is beneficial due to the anisotropic nature of Transformer representations and the presence of outlier dimensions.
The proposed layer-wise contribution measurement (based on distance to the output) significantly improves upon a previous norm-based approach.
Including the second layer normalization (from the feed-forward module) in the analysis has negligible impact on the faithfulness of the interpretations.
papers.limitation:
ALTI does not consider the classifier on top of the Transformer and therefore does not provide explanations for each of the output classes, unlike gradient-based methods.
Faithfulness is evaluated only via sufficiency and comprehensiveness metrics.
papers.abstract: The Transformer architecture aggregates input information through the self-attention mechanism, but there is no clear understanding of how this information is mixed across the entire model. Additionally, recent works have demonstrated that attention weights alone are not enough to describe the flow of information. In this paper, we consider the whole attention block --multi-head attention, residual connection, and layer normalization-- and define a metric to measure token-to-token interactions within each layer. Then, we aggregate layer-wise interpretations to provide input attribution scores for model predictions. Experimentally, we show that our method, ALTI (Aggregation of Layer-wise Token-to-token Interactions), provides more faithful explanations and increased robustness than gradient-based methods.

papers.title: Iteration Head: A Mechanistic Study of Chain-of-Thought
papers.research_question: How does Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning emerge in transformers, and what are the inner workings and conditions for its appearance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates how CoT reasoning emerges in transformers through the identification and analysis of a specialized attention mechanism called an 'iteration head', which enables efficient iterative reasoning.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can learn to solve iterative tasks efficiently via CoT reasoning by developing inner circuits (iteration heads) dedicated to multistep reasoning, and data curation can guide this process.
papers.key_findings:
Iteration heads, a specific pattern of weights in the first two attention layers, emerge in transformers trained on iterative tasks with CoT.
These heads enable the transformer to solve iterative tasks efficiently by retrieving the current input and previous state to compute the next state.
The iterative reasoning skill granted by iteration heads is transferable between different iterative tasks (e.g., from copying to parity).
Data curation (including easier tasks in training) can guide the model towards learning the iteration head circuit.
Transformers are stateless models, requiring generated states to have a token representation for CoT, which is a limitation for complex iterative algorithms.
papers.limitation: Transformers are stateless models, requiring generated states to have a token representation for CoT, which is a shortcoming for complex iterative algorithms or generic language modeling.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning is known to improve Large Language Models both empirically and in terms of theoretical approximation power. However, our understanding of the inner workings and conditions of apparition of CoT capabilities remains limited. This paper helps fill this gap by demonstrating how CoT reasoning emerges in transformers in a controlled and interpretable setting. In particular, we observe the appearance of a specialized attention mechanism dedicated to iterative reasoning, which we coined "iteration heads". We track both the emergence and the precise working of these iteration heads down to the attention level, and measure the transferability of the CoT skills to which they give rise between tasks.

papers.title: How Do LLMs Use Their Depth?
papers.research_question: How do LLMs internally structure their computations during inference and use their depth layer-by-layer to arrive at predictions?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a 'Guess-then-Refine' framework showing that LLMs use early layers for statistical guesses (high-frequency tokens) and later layers for contextual refinement, with depth usage varying by task complexity.
papers.conclusion: LLMs are early statistical guessers and late contextual integrators, using depth flexibly based on task complexity.
papers.key_findings:
Early LLM layers propose high-frequency tokens as statistical guesses due to lack of contextual information.
Early layer guesses are heavily refined in later layers, with 80% of early top-ranked guesses replaced.
In multiple-choice tasks, early layers collect valid options and later layers reason between them.
In multi-token fact recall, the first token requires more computational depth than subsequent tokens.
Function words (e.g., determiners, prepositions) are predicted correctly earlier than content words (nouns, verbs).
papers.limitation: Analysis limited to next-token prediction, fact recall, and downstream tasks; does not cover reasoning or chain-of-thought tasks.
future_direction: Analysis for reasoning and chain-of-thought tasks
Analysis of more recent reasoning models
papers.abstract: Growing evidence suggests that large language models do not use their depth uniformly, yet we still lack a fine-grained understanding of their layer-wise prediction dynamics. In this paper, we trace the intermediate representations of several open-weight models during inference and reveal a structured and nuanced use of depth. Specifically, we propose a "Guess-then-Refine" framework that explains how LLMs internally structure their computations to make predictions. We first show that the top-ranked predictions in early LLM layers are composed primarily of high-frequency tokens, which act as statistical guesses proposed by the model early on due to the lack of appropriate contextual information. As contextual information develops deeper into the model, these initial guesses get refined into contextually appropriate tokens. Even high-frequency token predictions from early layers get refined >70% of the time, indicating that correct token prediction is not "one-and-done". We then go beyond frequency-based prediction to examine the dynamic usage of layer depth across three case studies. (i) Part-of-speech analysis shows that function words are, on average, the earliest to be predicted correctly. (ii) Fact recall task analysis shows that, in a multi-token answer, the first token requires more computational depth than the rest. (iii) Multiple-choice task analysis shows that the model identifies the format of the response within the first half of the layers, but finalizes its response only toward the end. Together, our results provide a detailed view of depth usage in LLMs, shedding light on the layer-by-layer computations that underlie successful predictions and providing insights for future works to improve computational efficiency in transformer-based models.

papers.title: Small Vectors, Big Effects: A Mechanistic Study of RL-Induced Reasoning via Steering Vectors
papers.research_question: How does reasoning training reshape LLMs' internal computations, and what are the mechanisms of trainable steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: Lightweight steering vectors trained with an RL objective explain a large portion of full fine-tuning performance increase while preserving interpretability, and their mechanisms (e.g., token substitution at the last layer, MLP-mediated effects at the penultimate layer) are elucidated.
papers.conclusion: Steering vectors provide a compact and informative probe of reasoning-trained models, offering concrete insight into how RL-induced changes manifest in token preferences and internal circuitry.
papers.key_findings:
The last-layer steering vector acts like a token-substitution bias concentrated on the first generated token, boosting tokens such as 'To' and 'Step'.
The penultimate-layer vector leaves attention patterns largely intact and operates through the MLP and unembedding, up-weighting process words and structure symbols.
Steering vectors transfer to other models from the same family, suggesting underlying directions are preserved under fine-tuning.
Early-layer steering does not express later-layer steering directions; induced shifts diffuse and become nearly orthogonal to later-layer vectors.
Single-layer steering vectors isolate layer-specific effects and provide an upper bound on linear intervention performance at that layer.
papers.limitation: The effects are consistently stronger and cleaner in Qwen than in Llama, suggesting model-specific implementations of similar high-level behaviors.
future_direction: Systematic comparisons across architectures and training recipes to explain differences in steering vector effects.
Pin down the precise mechanisms of mid-layer steering vectors, which are harder to localize to a single submodule.
papers.abstract: The mechanisms by which reasoning training reshapes LLMs' internal computations remain unclear. We study lightweight steering vectors inserted into the base model's residual stream and trained with a reinforcement-learning objective. These vectors explain a large portion of full fine-tuning performance increase while preserving the interpretability of small, additive interventions. We find that (i) the last-layer steering vector acts like a token-substitution bias concentrated on the first generated token, consistently boosting tokens such as "To" and "Step"; (ii) the penultimate-layer vector leaves attention patterns largely intact and instead operates through the MLP and unembedding, preferentially up-weighting process words and structure symbols; and (iii) the steering vectors transfer to other models from the same family. Taken together, these results deepen understanding of how trained steering vectors shape computation and should inform future work in activation engineering and the study of reasoning models.

papers.title: Measuring Faithfulness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: Does chain-of-thought reasoning faithfully explain the model's actual reasoning process?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes tests for measuring faithfulness of chain-of-thought reasoning and finds that faithfulness varies across tasks and model sizes, with smaller models often producing more faithful reasoning.
papers.conclusion: Chain-of-thought reasoning is not always faithful, but it can be faithful under carefully chosen circumstances such as model size and task. Smaller models may be better to use if faithful reasoning is important.
papers.key_findings:
Models show large variation across tasks in how strongly they condition on the CoT when predicting their answer.
CoT's performance boost does not come from added test-time compute alone or from information encoded via the particular phrasing of the CoT.
As models become larger and more capable, they produce less faithful reasoning on most tasks studied.
Smaller models often generate more faithful reasoning than larger, more capable ones.
Faithfulness depends on model size and task difficulty, with easier tasks and larger models leading to less faithful reasoning.
papers.limitation:
Lack of ground truth about the model's internal reasoning process, making it impossible to know if CoT is truly faithful.
Analysis limited to RLHF-finetuned models; faithfulness may differ for pretrained LLMs or other training schemes.
future_direction: Investigate training schemes different from RLHF for eliciting more faithful reasoning.
Use the proposed metrics to increase the faithfulness of CoT and build systems with trustworthy reasoning.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) perform better when they produce step-by-step, "Chain-of-Thought" (CoT) reasoning before answering a question, but it is unclear if the stated reasoning is a faithful explanation of the model's actual reasoning (i.e., its process for answering the question). We investigate hypotheses for how CoT reasoning may be unfaithful, by examining how the model predictions change when we intervene on the CoT (e.g., by adding mistakes or paraphrasing it). Models show large variation across tasks in how strongly they condition on the CoT when predicting their answer, sometimes relying heavily on the CoT and other times primarily ignoring it. CoT's performance boost does not seem to come from CoT's added test-time compute alone or from information encoded via the particular phrasing of the CoT. As models become larger and more capable, they produce less faithful reasoning on most tasks we study. Overall, our results suggest that CoT can be faithful if the circumstances such as the model size and task are carefully chosen.

papers.title: What Do Self-Supervised Vision Transformers Learn?
papers.research_question: What do self-supervised vision transformers learn? Specifically, how and why contrastive learning (CL) and masked image modeling (MIM) differ in their representations and downstream task performance.
papers.core_contribution: CL and MIM learn complementary representations: CL captures global shape information but suffers from attention collapse, while MIM captures local texture information and preserves diversity. A simple linear combination of both losses can outperform each individually.
papers.conclusion: CL and MIM have opposing properties and are complementary; combining them can improve performance, and even a simple harmonization method shows benefits.
papers.key_findings:
CL trains self-attentions to capture global patterns and object shapes, but leads to attention collapse into homogeneity, reducing representation diversity.
MIM focuses on local patterns and textures, preserving token-level diversity and excelling in fine-tuning and dense prediction tasks.
CL utilizes low-frequency signals (shape-biased), while MIM utilizes high-frequency signals (texture-biased).
CL plays a crucial role in later layers, while MIM is important in early layers.
A simple linear combination of CL and MIM objectives can leverage the advantages of both methods, improving performance in linear probing and fine-tuning.
future_direction: Exploring better ways to combine CL and MIM than linear combination, such as applying CL in later layers and MIM in early layers.
Extending findings to multi-stage Vision Transformers like PiT and Swin.
Enhancing individual properties of CL and MIM to improve shape or texture learning.
papers.abstract: We present a comparative study on how and why contrastive learning (CL) and masked image modeling (MIM) differ in their representations and in their performance of downstream tasks. In particular, we demonstrate that self-supervised Vision Transformers (ViTs) have the following properties: (1) CL trains self-attentions to capture longer-range global patterns than MIM, such as the shape of an object, especially in the later layers of the ViT architecture. This CL property helps ViTs linearly separate images in their representation spaces. However, it also makes the self-attentions collapse into homogeneity for all query tokens and heads. Such homogeneity of self-attention reduces the diversity of representations, worsening scalability and dense prediction performance. (2) CL utilizes the low-frequency signals of the representations, but MIM utilizes high-frequencies. Since low- and high-frequency information respectively represent shapes and textures, CL is more shape-oriented and MIM more texture-oriented. (3) CL plays a crucial role in the later layers, while MIM mainly focuses on the early layers. Upon these analyses, we find that CL and MIM can complement each other and observe that even the simplest harmonization can help leverage the advantages of both methods. The code is available at https://github.com/naver-ai/cl-vs-mim.

papers.title: TokenSkip: Controllable Chain-of-Thought Compression in LLMs
papers.research_question: Does every token in the Chain-of-Thought (CoT) output contribute equally to deriving the answer? How can CoT sequences be compressed efficiently while preserving reasoning performance?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces TokenSkip, a method that enables LLMs to skip less important tokens in Chain-of-Thought sequences, allowing controllable compression with adjustable ratios, and demonstrates reduced token usage while preserving reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: TokenSkip is an effective approach for controllable Chain-of-Thought compression, balancing reasoning efficiency and accuracy, and offers valuable insights for advancing efficient CoT research.
papers.key_findings:
Tokens in CoT outputs have varying semantic importance, and skipping less important ones can compress CoT without significant performance drop.
TokenSkip reduces CoT tokens by 40% on GSM8K with less than 0.4% performance drop for Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct.
Larger models handle compression better with less performance degradation.
TokenSkip adheres well to specified compression ratios and outperforms baseline methods like truncation and prompt-based approaches.
TokenSkip maintains strong generalizability on out-of-domain tasks, such as commonsense reasoning.
papers.limitation:
Computational constraints prevented experiments with larger models (e.g., Qwen2.5-32B/72B) and long-CoT LLMs.
The token importance measurement (LLMLingua-2) was not trained on mathematical data, which may affect compression effectiveness.
future_direction: Explore TokenSkip on larger LLMs and long-CoT LLMs.
Improve token importance measurement for mathematical data.

papers.title: Do Latent-CoT Models Think Step-by-Step? A Mechanistic Study on Sequential Reasoning Tasks
papers.research_question: Does latent chain-of-thought (specifically CODI) implement genuine step-by-step reasoning on sequential tasks, or does it rely on shortcuts and late-stage fusion?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that latent CoT (CODI) implements step-by-step reasoning only for short hops (2-3) and shifts to a partial, late-bottleneck strategy for longer tasks, with performance and mechanism depending on the compressibility of the task (composite vs prime moduli).
papers.conclusion: With composite moduli, CODI is step-by-step on 2–3 hops but shifts to a late-intermediate partial rollout on longer horizons; with prime moduli, it largely fails to learn and shows neither signature. The split is explained by compressibility: composite moduli induce many-to-one contractions that bias the label toward late updates, making the computation compressible, while prime moduli lack this structure.
papers.key_findings:
For 2-3 hop polynomial tasks, CODI forms bridge states in the latent channel and fuses them with the final input at the answer readout.
For longer hop tasks (n>=4), CODI collapses to a partial latent rollout, representing only the last one or two intermediate states.
There is a prime-composite split: under composite moduli, CODI succeeds with a late-bottleneck strategy; under prime moduli, performance drops and step-by-step reasoning fails.
The final input is routed directly to the answer readout via a copy-like pathway, separate from the latent channel.
Teacher-guided compression drives the partial-reasoning strategy under composite moduli.
papers.limitation: CODI struggles with incompressible sequential tasks (e.g., prime moduli) due to fixed latent-compute budget.
future_direction: Test whether the compressibility dependence (including the prime–composite split) persists across latent-CoT objectives and architectures.
Develop adaptive mechanisms that allocate latent compute to match task demands.
Extend the mechanistic toolbox to more sequential and naturalistic datasets.
papers.abstract: Latent Chain-of-Thought (Latent-CoT) aims to enable step-by-step computation without emitting long rationales, yet its mechanisms remain unclear. We study CODI, a continuous-thought teacher-student distillation model, on strictly sequential polynomial-iteration tasks. Using logit-lens decoding, linear probes, attention analysis, and activation patching, we localize intermediate-state representations and trace their routing to the final readout. On two- and three-hop tasks, CODI forms the full set of bridge states that become decodable across latent-thought positions, while the final input follows a separate near-direct route; predictions arise via late fusion at the end-of-thought boundary. For longer hop lengths, CODI does not reliably execute a full latent rollout, instead exhibiting a partial latent reasoning path that concentrates on late intermediates and fuses them with the last input at the answer readout position. Ablations show that this partial pathway can collapse under regime shifts, including harder optimization. Overall, we delineate when CODI-style latent-CoT yields faithful iterative computation versus compressed or shortcut strategies, and highlight challenges in designing robust latent-CoT objectives for sequential reasoning.

papers.title: Self-Supervised Vision Transformers Learn Visual Concepts in Histopathology
papers.research_question: Can self-supervised learning, particularly DINO-based knowledge distillation, learn data-efficient and interpretable features in histology images?
papers.core_contribution: Vision Transformers using DINO-based self-supervised learning learn data-efficient and interpretable features in histology images, with different attention heads capturing distinct morphological phenotypes.
papers.conclusion: Self-supervised learning, particularly DINO, is effective for learning representations in histopathology, and the attention heads of Vision Transformers provide interpretable visual concepts that can aid in biomarker discovery.
papers.key_findings:
ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50 features are a strong baseline, achieving comparable performance to self-supervised methods on many tasks.
Self-supervised features, particularly from DINO, are robust and sample-efficient, performing well with less training data.
DINO outperforms SimCLR on weakly-supervised and patch-level tasks in histopathology.
DINO's attention heads learn distinct morphological visual concepts, localizing cells, stroma tissue, and fat/air pockets.
papers.limitation: Performance benefit of self-supervised learning may vary depending on organ type (only breast tissue tested) and weakly-supervised architecture (only CLAM tested).
future_direction: Assess the utility of self-supervised methods for learning representations of histopathological images from rare diseases with data paucity of slide-level and patch-level annotations.
papers.abstract: Tissue phenotyping is a fundamental task in learning objective characterizations of histopathologic biomarkers within the tumor-immune microenvironment in cancer pathology. However, whole-slide imaging (WSI) is a complex computer vision in which: 1) WSIs have enormous image resolutions with precludes large-scale pixel-level efforts in data curation, and 2) diversity of morphological phenotypes results in inter- and intra-observer variability in tissue labeling. To address these limitations, current efforts have proposed using pretrained image encoders (transfer learning from ImageNet, self-supervised pretraining) in extracting morphological features from pathology, but have not been extensively validated. In this work, we conduct a search for good representations in pathology by training a variety of self-supervised models with validation on a variety of weakly-supervised and patch-level tasks. Our key finding is in discovering that Vision Transformers using DINO-based knowledge distillation are able to learn data-efficient and interpretable features in histology images wherein the different attention heads learn distinct morphological phenotypes. We make evaluation code and pretrained weights publicly-available at: https://github.com/Richarizardd/Self-Supervised-ViT-Path.

papers.title: On the Interplay Between Fine-tuning and Sentence-level Probing for Linguistic Knowledge in Pre-trained Transformers
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning affect the representations and linguistic knowledge in pre-trained transformer models, and to what extent can changes in probing accuracy be attributed to changes in linguistic knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that fine-tuning pre-trained transformer models affects sentence-level probing accuracy, but these changes are not straightforward and often not due to acquisition or loss of linguistic knowledge; instead, they can be attributed to changes in attention distribution or other factors, requiring careful interpretation.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that fine-tuning can lead to substantial changes in probing accuracy, but these changes require careful interpretation as they may not directly indicate changes in linguistic knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning affects probing accuracy, with changes typically larger for higher layers.
Changes in probing accuracy vary across models, fine-tuning tasks, and probing tasks.
Improvements in probing accuracy with CLS-pooling can be attributed to changes in attention distribution rather than acquisition of new linguistic knowledge.
Fine-tuning can negatively affect probing accuracy, possibly due to changes in representations.
Only in few cases does fine-tuning improve probing accuracy beyond using a strong pooling method like mean-pooling.
papers.limitation: It remains unclear whether fine-tuning indeed removes the linguistic knowledge or whether it is simply no longer linearly separable.
future_direction: Further investigation into whether fine-tuning removes linguistic knowledge or just makes it not linearly separable.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning pre-trained contextualized embedding models has become an integral part of the NLP pipeline. At the same time, probing has emerged as a way to investigate the linguistic knowledge captured by pre-trained models. Very little is, however, understood about how fine-tuning affects the representations of pre-trained models and thereby the linguistic knowledge they encode. This paper contributes towards closing this gap. We study three different pre-trained models: BERT, RoBERTa, and ALBERT, and investigate through sentence-level probing how finetuning affects their representations. We find that for some probing tasks fine-tuning leads to substantial changes in accuracy, possibly suggesting that fine-tuning introduces or even removes linguistic knowledge from a pre-trained model. These changes, however, vary greatly across different models, fine-tuning and probing tasks. Our analysis reveals that while finetuning indeed changes the representations of a pre-trained model and these changes are typically larger for higher layers, only in very few cases, fine-tuning has a positive effect on probing accuracy that is larger than just using the pre-trained model with a strong pooling method. Based on our findings, we argue that both positive and negative effects of finetuning on probing require a careful interpretation.

papers.title: Liquid Reasoning Transformers: A Sudoku-Based Prototype for Chess-Scale Algorithmic Tasks
papers.research_question: How can transformers be designed to perform iterative, adaptive-depth reasoning for structured problems like Sudoku and chess?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Liquid Reasoning Transformer, an architecture that performs iterative, adaptive-depth inference for structured reasoning tasks, demonstrated on Sudoku with high accuracy without symbolic rules or search.
papers.conclusion: The Liquid Reasoning Transformer enables adaptive-depth iterative reasoning for structured problems, achieving strong performance on Sudoku and providing a framework for extensions to tasks like chess.
papers.key_findings:
Achieves 98.68% digit accuracy and 36.30% puzzle accuracy on Sudoku without using symbolic rules or search.
Learns to allocate computation adaptively using a stop gate, with more steps for difficult puzzles.
Uses a discard gate to filter incorrect intermediate hypotheses, improving stability.
Internal reasoning patterns show convergence and correction of errors over iterative steps.
Demonstrates that transformers can benefit from explicit internal reasoning steps for structured tasks.
papers.limitation:
Fixed maximum depth for reasoning loop restricts ability to resolve long or highly branched inference chains.
Single recurrent reasoning token limits capacity to maintain multiple parallel hypotheses or track several long-range dependencies.
Discard mechanism may become unstable in more complex tasks, potentially discarding useful information or relying too much on aggressive pruning.
High computational cost due to gating and repeated transformer passes, requiring optimization for scaling.
Sudoku may not generalize directly to chess without additional modifications due to complexity differences.
future_direction: Extending the architecture to chess-scale reasoning tasks.
Exploring multi-token reasoning states.
Investigating reinforcement learning approaches or training on sequences of moves for advanced tactical understanding.
papers.abstract: The Liquid Reasoning Transformer (LRT) is a transformer architecture designed for inference with adaptive depths using iterative changes, discard-based correction, and a learned stopping mechanism. Instead of relying on a single feedforward pass, the model updates a recurrent reasoning token across multiple internal steps, allowing it to correct early errors and allocate computation based on input difficulty. We evaluate the LRT on Sudoku as a controlled testbed for structured reasoning and show that it achieves strong performance, reaching 98.68% digit accuracy and 36.30% full-puzzle accuracy without using symbolic rules or search. Analyzing internal patterns shows that the discard and stop gates play different, important roles in stabilizing inferences and adjusting computational depth. We discuss how these mechanisms extend naturally to chess-scale reasoning tasks and outline extensions for multi-token reasoning and larger domains.

papers.title: Does Circuit Analysis Interpretability Scale? Evidence from Multiple Choice Capabilities in Chinchilla
papers.research_question: Does circuit analysis interpretability scale to large language models, specifically for the algorithmic task of multiple-choice question answering?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that existing circuit analysis techniques (logit attribution, attention pattern visualization, activation patching) scale to a 70B parameter model, allowing identification and partial understanding of the circuit for multiple-choice question answering, particularly 'correct letter' heads.
papers.conclusion: Circuit analysis techniques can scale to large models, but the features used to implement algorithmic tasks can be messy in their semantics, even when limited to a distribution with little superposition.
papers.key_findings:
Identified 45 nodes (attention heads and MLPs) that are causally responsible for most of the model's performance on the multiple-choice task.
Categorized attention heads into four types: 'Correct Letter', 'Uniform', 'Single Letter', and 'Amplification'.
Found that 'correct letter' heads attend to the correct answer label and copy it to the output logits.
Used SVD to compress query/key/value subspaces of 'correct letter' heads, finding the query and key subspaces represent an 'Nth item in an enumeration' feature, but this is only a partial explanation for behavior on a more general distribution.
Showed that the algorithmic task of mapping the correct answer to its label is interpretable, but the specific features used are messy and only partially understood.
papers.limitation:
The effect of patching a node can be compensated by downstream nodes (backup behavior), potentially distorting results.
The analysis only finds a cross-section of the circuit (nodes separating ancestors and descendants) rather than the full set of relevant nodes.
Results are only applicable to the specific distribution tested (MMLU subset).
Focused on the net effect on the correct label, neglecting the part of the circuit that identifies the set of possible answer tokens.
future_direction: Investigating the rest of the circuit (nodes feeding into the correct letter heads).
Comparing different approaches to causal interventions (e.g., noising vs. denoising).
Automating circuit analysis to reduce labor intensity.
papers.abstract: \emph{Circuit analysis} is a promising technique for understanding the internal mechanisms of language models. However, existing analyses are done in small models far from the state of the art. To address this, we present a case study of circuit analysis in the 70B Chinchilla model, aiming to test the scalability of circuit analysis. In particular, we study multiple-choice question answering, and investigate Chinchilla's capability to identify the correct answer \emph{label} given knowledge of the correct answer \emph{text}. We find that the existing techniques of logit attribution, attention pattern visualization, and activation patching naturally scale to Chinchilla, allowing us to identify and categorize a small set of `output nodes' (attention heads and MLPs). We further study the `correct letter' category of attention heads aiming to understand the semantics of their features, with mixed results. For normal multiple-choice question answers, we significantly compress the query, key and value subspaces of the head without loss of performance when operating on the answer labels for multiple-choice questions, and we show that the query and key subspaces represent an `Nth item in an enumeration' feature to at least some extent. However, when we attempt to use this explanation to understand the heads' behaviour on a more general distribution including randomized answer labels, we find that it is only a partial explanation, suggesting there is more to learn about the operation of `correct letter' heads on multiple choice question answering.

papers.title: Supernova: Achieving More with Less in Transformer Architectures
papers.research_question: How can careful architectural design and tokenization innovation achieve the performance of larger transformer models while maintaining computational efficiency?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Supernova, a 650M parameter decoder-only transformer that achieves ~90% of the performance of 1B parameter models using 35% fewer parameters and only 100B training tokens, demonstrating that architectural efficiency and tokenization quality can compensate for reduced scale.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that the future of economically viable AI lies in thoughtful architectural design and engineering excellence, proving that the sub-billion parameter regime remains rich with untapped potential and enabling sustainable AI deployment.
papers.key_findings:
Supernova achieves approximately 90% of the performance of leading 1B parameter models while using 35% fewer parameters.
The model requires only 100B training tokens, an order of magnitude less than competitors, demonstrating exceptional data efficiency.
The custom 128,000-vocabulary byte-level BPE tokenizer achieves state-of-the-art compression performance (4.78 characters per token on WikiText-103).
The combination of RoPE, GQA, RMSNorm, and SwiGLU creates synergistic effects that exceed the sum of individual optimizations.
Inference efficiency metrics show 59.6% higher throughput, 35.7% lower memory usage, and 36.8% lower cost per 1M tokens compared to a 1B parameter baseline.
papers.limitation:
English-only constraint due to tokenizer optimization limits multilingual capabilities.
Context length of 2048 tokens may be insufficient for some applications requiring longer context.
Performance on highly technical domains could be improved with domain-specific fine-tuning.
Instruction following would require fine-tuning for optimal chat and instruction-following applications.
future_direction: Develop language-specific models with optimized tokenizers for other major languages.
Investigate RoPE scaling techniques and other approaches for extending context length while maintaining efficiency.
Explore scaling the model size for further performance gains.
papers.abstract: We present Supernova, a 650M-parameter decoder-only transformer that demonstrates how careful architectural design and tokenization innovation can achieve the performance of larger models while maintaining computational efficiency. Our architecture combines Rotary Positional Embeddings (RoPE), Grouped Query Attention (GQA) with a 3:1 compression ratio, RMSNorm for computational efficiency, and SwiGLU activation functions. A critical innovation is our custom 128,000-vocabulary byte-level BPE tokenizer, which achieves state-of-the-art compression performance. Through detailed analysis, we show that Supernova achieves 90% of the performance of 1B-parameter models while using 35% fewer parameters and requiring only 100B training tokens--an order of magnitude less than competing models. Our findings challenge the prevailing scaling paradigm, demonstrating that architectural efficiency and tokenization quality can compensate for reduced parameter counts.

papers.title: Language Models Represent Space and Time
papers.research_question: Do large language models learn coherent linear representations of space and time, i.e., do they form a world model?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models learn linear representations of space and time that are robust to prompting and unified across entity types, and individual 'space' and 'time' neurons exist that encode these coordinates.
papers.conclusion: Modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes can recover spatial and temporal coordinates from internal activations, with performance increasing with model size and plateauing in middle layers.
Spatial and temporal features are linearly represented, as nonlinear probes do not improve performance.
Representations are robust to variations in prompting, though random tokens or capitalization degrade performance.
Probes generalize across entity types and to held-out geographic or temporal blocks, indicating unified representations.
Individual neurons exist that are highly predictive of space and time, and causal interventions confirm their importance.
papers.limitation:
Data comes only from English Wikipedia, skewing towards the Anglosphere, and entity type distribution is not uniform.
The true extent and structure of spatial and temporal representations remain unclear.
future_direction: Extracting representations in the model’s coordinate system rather than human coordinates, e.g., with sparse autoencoders.
Studying how these spatiotemporal representations are learned, recalled, and used internally across training checkpoints.
Investigating potential parallels with biological place and grid cells in the brain.
papers.abstract: The capabilities of large language models (LLMs) have sparked debate over whether such systems just learn an enormous collection of superficial statistics or a set of more coherent and grounded representations that reflect the real world. We find evidence for the latter by analyzing the learned representations of three spatial datasets (world, US, NYC places) and three temporal datasets (historical figures, artworks, news headlines) in the Llama-2 family of models. We discover that LLMs learn linear representations of space and time across multiple scales. These representations are robust to prompting variations and unified across different entity types (e.g. cities and landmarks). In addition, we identify individual "space neurons" and "time neurons" that reliably encode spatial and temporal coordinates. While further investigation is needed, our results suggest modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.

papers.title: Back Attention: Understanding and Enhancing Multi-Hop Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models perform latent multi-hop reasoning, and how can this ability be enhanced?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces back attention, a novel mechanism that allows lower layers to capture higher-layer hidden states, enhancing multi-hop reasoning in LLMs. Also introduces logit flow, an interpretability method for tracing logit propagation.
papers.conclusion: The analysis provides new insights into multi-hop reasoning mechanisms and introduces back attention, a powerful and lightweight method that significantly enhances reasoning accuracy in LLMs by allowing lower layers to access higher-layer features.
papers.key_findings:
Identifies four distinct stages in single-hop knowledge prediction: entity subject enrichment, entity attribute extraction, relation subject enrichment, and relation attribute extraction.
Finds that failures in multi-hop reasoning often stem from the relation attribute extraction stage, where conflicting logits reduce prediction accuracy.
Proposes back attention, which enables a 1-layer transformer to achieve the performance of a 2-layer transformer on arithmetic tasks.
Back attention, when fine-tuned on a single layer of pre-trained LLMs, significantly improves accuracy across five reasoning datasets and four different models.
Logit flow provides a neuron-level perspective on information flow, offering a more granular understanding than layer-level methods like activation patching.
papers.limitation:
The interpretability analysis primarily focuses on single-hop and two-hop knowledge queries, which represent specific reasoning scenarios; other reasoning tasks might involve different mechanisms.
Back attention is applied to only a single layer in this work, though it could be extended to two or more layers for potentially greater improvements.
future_direction: Extend back attention to two or more layers.
Validate the findings on more diverse reasoning tasks to refine the interpretability framework for broader applicability.
papers.abstract: We investigate how large language models perform latent multi-hop reasoning in prompts like "Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart's mother's spouse is". To analyze this process, we introduce logit flow, an interpretability method that traces how logits propagate across layers and positions toward the final prediction. Using logit flow, we identify four distinct stages in single-hop knowledge prediction: (A) entity subject enrichment, (B) entity attribute extraction, (C) relation subject enrichment, and (D) relation attribute extraction. Extending this analysis to multi-hop reasoning, we find that failures often stem from the relation attribute extraction stage, where conflicting logits reduce prediction accuracy. To address this, we propose back attention, a novel mechanism that enables lower layers to leverage higher-layer hidden states from different positions during attention computation. With back attention, a 1-layer transformer achieves the performance of a 2-layer transformer. Applied to four LLMs, back attention improves accuracy on five reasoning datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in enhancing latent multi-hop reasoning ability.

papers.title: In Their Own Words: Reasoning Traces Tailored for Small Models Make Them Better Reasoners
papers.abstract: Transferring reasoning capabilities from larger language models to smaller ones through supervised fine-tuning often fails counterintuitively, with performance degrading despite access to high-quality teacher demonstrations. We identify that this failure stems from distributional misalignment: reasoning traces from larger models contain tokens that are low probability under the student's distribution, exceeding the internal representation capacity of smaller architectures and creating learning barriers rather than helpful guidance. We propose Reverse Speculative Decoding (RSD), a mechanism for generating student-friendly reasoning traces in which the teacher model proposes candidate tokens but the student model determines acceptance based on its own probability distributions, filtering low probability tokens. When applied to Qwen3-0.6B, direct distillation of s1K-1.1 reasoning trace data degrades average performance across major reasoning benchmarks by 20.5\%, while the same model trained on RSD-generated reasoning traces achieves meaningful improvements of 4.9\%. Our analysis reveals that low probability tokens constitute the critical bottleneck in reasoning ability transfer. However, cross-model experiments demonstrate that RSD traces are model-specific rather than universally applicable, indicating that distributional alignment must be tailored for each student architecture's unique internal representation.

papers.title: What Layers When: Learning to Skip Compute in LLMs with Residual Gates
papers.research_question: How can we enable token-wise layer skipping in decoder-only language models to save compute while maintaining accuracy?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces GateSkip, a residual gating mechanism that enables token-wise layer skipping in decoder-only transformers, achieving compute savings while maintaining or improving accuracy.
papers.conclusion: GateSkip turns the residual stream into a stable and practical control mechanism for adaptive depth, offering real efficiency gains without sacrificing stability or performance.
papers.key_findings:
GateSkip saves up to 15% compute on long-form reasoning tasks while retaining >90% of baseline accuracy.
On instruction-tuned models, GateSkip improves accuracy at full compute and matches baseline quality with nearly 50% compute savings.
The learned gates provide insight into transformer information flow, e.g., BOS tokens and punctuation act as anchors.
GateSkip is compatible with orthogonal efficiency techniques like quantization, pruning, and self-speculative decoding.
The method is stable and can be fine-tuned on top of pretrained models without destabilizing optimization.
papers.limitation: Targets 1-8B parameter decoder-only LLMs and evaluates on English reasoning, translation, and general language modeling.
papers.abstract: We introduce GateSkip, a simple residual-stream gating mechanism that enables token-wise layer skipping in decoder-only LMs. Each Attention/MLP branch is equipped with a sigmoid-linear gate that condenses the branch's output before it re-enters the residual stream. During inference we rank tokens by the gate values and skip low-importance ones using a per-layer budget. While early-exit or router-based Mixture-of-Depths models are known to be unstable and need extensive retraining, our smooth, differentiable gates fine-tune stably on top of pretrained models. On long-form reasoning, we save up to 15% compute while retaining over 90% of baseline accuracy. For increasingly larger models, this tradeoff improves drastically. On instruction-tuned models we see accuracy gains at full compute and match baseline quality near 50% savings. The learned gates give insight into transformer information flow (e.g., BOS tokens act as anchors), and the method combines easily with quantization, pruning, and self-speculative decoding.

papers.title: Behind the Scene: Revealing the Secrets of Pre-trained Vision-and-Language Models
papers.research_question: How do pre-trained vision-and-language models work internally? Specifically, the paper investigates multimodal fusion, modality importance, cross-modal interaction, visual relations, and linguistic knowledge in these models.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces VALUE, a set of probing tasks for vision-and-language models, and uses it to analyze UNITER and LXMERT, revealing that textual modality is more dominant, a subset of heads specialize in cross-modal interaction, and visual relations and linguistic knowledge are encoded.
papers.conclusion: The analysis provides insights into the inner workings of pre-trained V+L models and offers guidelines for future model design, such as preferring single-stream architecture and initializing with BERT weights.
papers.key_findings:
Pre-trained models attend more to text than images during inference.
A subset of attention heads are tailored for capturing cross-modal interactions.
Learned attention matrices show patterns coherent with latent alignment between image regions and textual words.
Attention patterns reveal visually-interpretable relations among image regions.
Linguistic knowledge is effectively encoded in the attention heads.
future_direction: Perform model compression via pruning attention heads based on the analysis.
papers.abstract: Recent Transformer-based large-scale pre-trained models have revolutionized vision-and-language (V+L) research. Models such as ViLBERT, LXMERT and UNITER have significantly lifted state of the art across a wide range of V+L benchmarks with joint image-text pre-training. However, little is known about the inner mechanisms that destine their impressive success. To reveal the secrets behind the scene of these powerful models, we present VALUE (Vision-And-Language Understanding Evaluation), a set of meticulously designed probing tasks (e.g., Visual Coreference Resolution, Visual Relation Detection, Linguistic Probing Tasks) generalizable to standard pre-trained V+L models, aiming to decipher the inner workings of multimodal pre-training (e.g., the implicit knowledge garnered in individual attention heads, the inherent cross-modal alignment learned through contextualized multimodal embeddings). Through extensive analysis of each archetypal model architecture via these probing tasks, our key observations are: (i) Pre-trained models exhibit a propensity for attending over text rather than images during inference. (ii) There exists a subset of attention heads that are tailored for capturing cross-modal interactions. (iii) Learned attention matrix in pre-trained models demonstrates patterns coherent with the latent alignment between image regions and textual words. (iv) Plotted attention patterns reveal visually-interpretable relations among image regions. (v) Pure linguistic knowledge is also effectively encoded in the attention heads. These are valuable insights serving to guide future work towards designing better model architecture and objectives for multimodal pre-training.

papers.title: Quantifying Language Models' Sensitivity to Spurious Features in Prompt Design or: How I learned to start worrying about prompt formatting
papers.research_question: How sensitive are large language models to subtle, meaning-preserving changes in prompt formatting?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that LLMs are extremely sensitive to semantically equivalent prompt formatting choices, and introduces FORMAT SPREAD, a method to efficiently estimate the performance spread across plausible formats without accessing model weights.
papers.conclusion: The paper argues that research evaluating LLMs with prompting should report performance across a range of plausible prompt formats rather than a single format, and that FORMAT SPREAD facilitates this systematic analysis.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs show extreme sensitivity to prompt formatting, with performance differences of up to 76 accuracy points between equivalent formats.
Sensitivity persists even when increasing model size, the number of few-shot examples, or with instruction tuning.
Format performance only weakly correlates between models, questioning the validity of comparing models with a single, fixed prompt format.
Small atomic changes in format (e.g., casing, separators) can lead to large, unpredictable accuracy changes.
Prompt formats are highly identifiable from the model's internal representations (prompt embeddings), and this identifiability correlates with performance spread.
papers.limitation: Some generated prompt formats may be unnatural (e.g., due to parsing choices or unusual separators), and the study is limited to tasks with reasonably short input instructions and field length.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are adopted as a fundamental component of language technologies, it is crucial to accurately characterize their performance. Because choices in prompt design can strongly influence model behavior, this design process is critical in effectively using any modern pre-trained generative language model. In this work, we focus on LLM sensitivity to a quintessential class of meaning-preserving design choices: prompt formatting. We find that several widely used open-source LLMs are extremely sensitive to subtle changes in prompt formatting in few-shot settings, with performance differences of up to 76 accuracy points when evaluated using LLaMA-2-13B. Sensitivity remains even when increasing model size, the number of few-shot examples, or performing instruction tuning. Our analysis suggests that work evaluating LLMs with prompting-based methods would benefit from reporting a range of performance across plausible prompt formats, instead of the currently-standard practice of reporting performance on a single format. We also show that format performance only weakly correlates between models, which puts into question the methodological validity of comparing models with an arbitrarily chosen, fixed prompt format. To facilitate systematic analysis we propose FormatSpread, an algorithm that rapidly evaluates a sampled set of plausible prompt formats for a given task, and reports the interval of expected performance without accessing model weights.
